title: Interest
concept: Interest is an amount added to money over time. Savers may earn interest, while borrowers usually pay interest.
learningObjective: Understand that interest can increase savings balances and make borrowed money more expensive to repay.
secondaryMisconceptions: Savers and borrowers experience interest in the same way.
A borrower only needs to repay the original amount borrowed.
keyTakeaway: Interest can help savers and cost borrowers.

screens.title: The Same Increase, Two Reactions
screens.content: Two people start with Rs. 10,000. After one year, both balances rise—but only one person is happier. Why?
screens.illustration: Two children stand beside identical Rs. 10,000 balance cards. One card has a saving jar; the other has a repayment note.

screens.title: Save or Borrow?
screens.content: Sara saves Rs. 10,000 in a bank account. Hamza borrows Rs. 10,000 with his family to pay for a necessary repair.
screens.illustration: Sara places money into a bank account while Hamza and a parent receive a loan for a repair.

screens.title: One Simple Game Rate
screens.content: For this game, both examples use a simple 10% yearly rate. That means Rs. 1,000 is added after one year.
screens.illustration: A simple card shows: 10% of Rs. 10,000 = Rs. 1,000.

screens.title: Higher Does Not Mean Better
screens.content: The saver’s balance grows. The borrower’s amount owed also grows. The same increase has two very different meanings.
screens.illustration: Sara’s saving jar rises happily while Hamza’s repayment note becomes larger.

screens.title: What Will Change?
screens.question: After one year, what will most likely happen in this activity?

options.text: Both balances rise, but for different reasons
options.response: Good prediction. One increase belongs to the saver, while the other becomes an extra cost for the borrower.
Savings may grow, but interest can also increase the amount a borrower owes.
A saver may receive interest. A borrower usually pays it.
The original amount is called the principal. Interest may be added to what must be repaid.

screens.title: One Year Later
screens.instruction: Complete both before-and-after comparisons. Then decide whether the added interest helps or costs each person.

educationalAssumptions: Both use a simple 10% rate for one year.
Ten per cent of Rs. 10,000 is Rs. 1,000.
The activity uses the same rate only to make the comparison easy.
No extra deposits, withdrawals, fees, missed payments, or compounding are included.
Real savings and loan rates may differ.
The example does not promise that a real bank will offer this return or loan rate.

comparisons.title: Saving Money
comparisons.learnerQuestion: What will Sara’s balance be after Rs. 1,000 of interest is added?
comparisons.explanation: Sara earns interest in this activity. The added money increases the balance she owns.

comparisons.title: Borrowing Money
comparisons.learnerQuestion: What will Hamza owe after Rs. 1,000 of interest is charged?

afterState.effect: Hamza must repay Rs. 1,000 more than he borrowed.

comparisons.explanation: Hamza pays interest in this activity. The added amount increases his repayment cost.

finalLearnerQuestion.text: Both balances became Rs. 11,000. What is the important difference?

options.text: Sara owns Rs. 11,000; Hamza owes Rs. 11,000
Hamza no longer needs to repay anything

importantHiddenDifference: Sara has more money that belongs to her.
Hamza has more money that he must repay.
config.validationMethod: Check each after-value and the final hidden-difference answer. Complete the interaction when all three answers are correct.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correct answers marked. Return only the incorrect comparison, show the calculation, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present each comparison as a linear text card with radio-button answers. Read the before amount, interest amount, and after options aloud.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Listen to the starting amount and interest. Choose the final balance, then decide whether the person owns or owes it.

feedback.success: Excellent comparison. The same Rs. 1,000 increase helps Sara but increases Hamza’s repayment.
feedback.incorrect: Look at whether the balance is money the person owns or money the person owes.
feedback.incomplete: Complete both comparisons and identify the hidden difference before finishing.

screens.title: Interest Changes a Balance
screens.content: You saw both balances rise from Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 11,000. The added Rs. 1,000 is interest. Interest is an amount added to money over time. A saver may earn it, so the savings balance grows. A borrower usually pays it, so the amount owed grows. Interest is not always free money: its effect depends on whether you are saving or borrowing. Real rates, time periods, fees, and calculation methods vary.
screens.simpleSummary: Interest can grow savings or increase what a borrower must repay.
screens.illustration: One Rs. 1,000 arrow moves into Sara’s saving jar. Another Rs. 1,000 arrow is added to Hamza’s repayment note.

screens.title: The Bicycle Comparison
screens.content: Mariam saves Rs. 5,000 and earns Rs. 250 under a practice account rate. Her balance becomes Rs. 5,250. Daniyal borrows Rs. 5,000 and is charged Rs. 250. He must repay Rs. 5,250. The same interest amount helps one and costs the other.
screens.illustration: A saving jar and a bicycle-repair loan both move from Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 5,250, with Owned and Owed labels.

questions.text: A savings balance rises from Rs. 2,000 to Rs. 2,100 without another deposit. What most likely caused the extra Rs. 100?

options.feedback: Correct. In this example, the extra Rs. 100 was interest added over time.
Borrowed money creates an amount to repay. It is different from interest earned on savings.
A withdrawal removes money and would normally make the balance lower.
The starting money remains in the account. The balance rose because an additional amount was added.

questions.correctExplanation: The saver did not add more money. In this example, the extra Rs. 100 was interest added over time.
questions.misconceptionTested: Savers and borrowers experience interest in the same way.

questions.text: A family borrows Rs. 5,000 and is charged Rs. 500 interest. How much must they repay in this simple example?

options.feedback: Interest is added to the borrowed amount in this example; it is not subtracted.
Rs. 5,000 is only the original amount borrowed. The Rs. 500 interest must also be repaid.
Correct. The original Rs. 5,000 plus Rs. 500 interest equals Rs. 5,500.
The amount does not automatically double. Add the stated Rs. 500 interest to Rs. 5,000.

questions.correctExplanation: The borrower repays the original Rs. 5,000 plus Rs. 500 of interest.
questions.misconceptionTested: A borrower only needs to repay the original amount borrowed.

questions.text: Amina saves Rs. 3,000 and earns Rs. 300 interest. Bilal borrows Rs. 3,000 and is charged Rs. 300 interest. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Amina owns Rs. 3,300; Bilal owes Rs. 3,300
options.feedback: Correct. The same interest amount helps Amina’s savings but increases Bilal’s repayment.
Amina earned interest, but Bilal was charged interest.
Bilal owes the original Rs. 3,000 plus the Rs. 300 interest charge.

options.text: Interest was free money for both
options.feedback: The interest helps Amina’s savings but is an extra cost for Bilal.

questions.correctExplanation: Amina’s interest increases money she owns. Bilal’s interest increases money he must repay.

screens.headline: Interest Investigator!
screens.message: You discovered why interest can grow a saver’s balance while increasing a borrower’s repayment.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 9 complete in Make Money Grow.
screens.nextMissionTeaser: Next, discover how earning interest for longer can change the final amount.
screens.animation: Two Rs. 10,000 cards rise to Rs. 11,000. One enters a saving jar while the other attaches to a repayment note.

screens.title: Owned or Owed?
screens.instruction: Draw two boxes labelled Savings and Borrowing. Add an imaginary Rs. 100 interest to each and write whether the new amount is owned or owed.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on how interest affects savings and borrowed money.
The calculations correctly apply the clearly stated simple 10% classroom rate for one year.
The mission uses simple numbers, family support, saving, repairs, and clear owned-versus-owed comparisons.
The mission explains a general concept without recommending a real account, loan, or financial product.
The 10% rate is clearly labelled as an educational activity assumption rather than a promised real return.
The mission does not discuss stocks or market prices.
Borrowing is presented neutrally as a tool that creates repayment rather than as a personal failure.
The mission states that real rates may differ and excludes fees, compounding, missed payments, and other transactions from the simplified comparison.
The mission uses Pakistani rupees, savings accounts, family borrowing, and necessary repairs.
The learner calculates both final balances and identifies the difference between money owned and money owed.
The quiz addresses interest on savings, repayment of principal plus interest, and the idea that interest is always free money.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, two simple comparisons, one hidden-difference question, and three concise quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The wording is concrete, supportive, and suitable for children aged 8–12.
